correctness.rationale: For any origin-interior convex body, the uniform radial sandwich gives |p log(rho_{K+y/p}/rho_K)| <= const on bounded y; at a.e. smooth radial boundary point it tends to (y·normal)/(z·normal). The polar integral yields the log-cosh limit after the odd term cancels by divergence theorem. Uniform Lipschitz control in y gives local uniformity. The negative-power mean lies between intersection radius and 2^(1/p) times intersection radius; the first variation of the ordinary covariogram gives a uniform brightness-norm lower bound near zero and rules out remote sublevels, so local uniform limits imply global Hausdorff for each fixed tau>0. Hessian positive on every nonzero vector via full-dimensional normal support; coercivity via log cosh >= |t|-log 2. Facet formula and strict majorization of log cosh(sqrt(s)) yield exact cubical John/Löwner radii and contact sets. Independently reproduced square polar quadrature at y=(0.9,-0.4), p=25,100,500,2000 approaches 4[log cosh(.45)+log cosh(.2)]=0.4714990640 with p=2000 estimate 0.4714789693; experiments only corroborate.
residual_risks: The a.e. tangent-plane expansion and uniform covariogram brightness lower bound are standard convex-geometric ingredients; no quantitative rate or uniformity over varying K is established.

value.rationale: Removing all boundary regularity from the exact critical transition answers a natural sharp-boundary case left open by the C^3 theorem: facets/edges form basic convex examples not covered by its differentiability argument. Global rather than local Hausdorff convergence is mathematically substantive, and the orthotope normal formula supplies explicit reference geometry. The claim is not just a rebranding of the known log-cosh functional.
